overview.title: Retraining for nine epochs and the random baseline
overview.section: 4.2 Classifying newswires: A multiclass classification example
overview.main_topic: Retraining the Reuters model from scratch for nine epochs, evaluating it on the test set (≈80% accuracy), and comparing with a shuffled-label random baseline (≈19%)
overview.central_idea: Using the epoch count chosen from the validation curves, a fresh model trained on all training data reaches about 80% test accuracy, far above the roughly 19% a random classifier would get on this imbalanced 46-class problem.
overview.importance: It completes the validate → choose hyperparameter → retrain → test cycle, and introduces the habit of judging a score against a trivial baseline rather than in isolation.
learning_objectives: Explain why the model is rebuilt from scratch rather than continued from the 20-epoch run
Interpret the two numbers returned by `model.evaluate()`
Explain why the random baseline for 46 imbalanced classes is not 1/46
Implement a shuffled-label random baseline and relate it to the class distribution
prerequisites: Figures 4.6-4.8 (p.145-146) showing overfitting after about nine epochs
Listings 4.15-4.16 (p.143-144) for the model and compile settings

summary:
From the curves on p.145-146 the authors conclude: **"The model begins to overfit after nine epochs."** They therefore build a **new model from scratch** (listing 4.22) with the same architecture as listing 4.15 (Dense 64 relu → Dense 64 relu → Dense 46 softmax), compile it with Adam and categorical crossentropy, and this time monitor only `"accuracy"` (top-3 is dropped). It is trained on the **full** training set (`x_train`, `y_train`, all 8,982 samples, no validation split) for `epochs=9` with `batch_size=512`, and then scored with `model.evaluate(x_test, y_test)`.

The result is `[0.9565213431445807, 0.79697239536954589]`: a test loss of about 0.96 and a **test accuracy of about 80%**.

Is 80% good? The authors point out that for a balanced binary problem a random classifier would get 50%, but with 46 classes that "may not be equally represented" the right reference point is less obvious. They estimate it empirically: copy the test labels, shuffle the copy with `np.random.shuffle`, compare element-wise with the original labels, and average the resulting booleans. The result, **0.1866**, means a random classifier that respects the label frequencies would be right about **19%** of the time. Against that baseline, 80% is clearly meaningful.

Note (not in the book): 19% is far above $1/46\approx2.2\%$ because Reuters topics are heavily imbalanced; a shuffled-label baseline has expected accuracy $\sum_k p_k^2$, which is dominated by the few largest topics. The book develops the idea of common-sense baselines more generally on p.176.

paragraphs.excerpt: The model begins to overfit after nine epochs. Let’s train a new
paragraphs.what_it_says: Reading the validation curves, the authors put the onset of overfitting at nine epochs and decide to train a fresh model for nine epochs, then evaluate it on the test set.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The validation run served only to choose a hyperparameter (the epoch count). The final model is a new one, so it does not carry the over-trained weights from the 20-epoch run. It is also trained on all 8,982 training samples, since the validation split is no longer needed.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the standard pattern: tune on validation, then retrain and measure once on the test set. Stopping at the validation-loss minimum is a manual form of early stopping.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Nine epochs matches the minimum of validation loss in figure 4.6 (p.145). Training on 8,982 rather than 7,982 samples changes the number of updates per epoch (18 instead of 16), so the "best" epoch count is only approximately transferable.

paragraphs.excerpt: This approach reaches an accuracy of approximately 80%. With a balanced binary
paragraphs.what_it_says: The model gets about 80% test accuracy. For balanced binary classification, random guessing gives 50%, but here there are 46 possibly unequal classes, so the authors propose to measure a random baseline empirically.
paragraphs.what_it_means: An accuracy number is meaningful only relative to what a trivial strategy achieves. With imbalanced classes, the trivial reference depends on the class frequencies, not just on the number of classes.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This guards against over- or under-interpreting a metric, a habit the book returns to in chapter 5 (p.176).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Shuffling the labels keeps the class frequencies but destroys any relation to the inputs, simulating a classifier that guesses classes at their base rates.

concepts.name: Random (shuffled-label) baseline
concepts.definition: The accuracy obtained by predicting labels at random while matching the class frequencies, estimated here by comparing the test labels with a shuffled copy.
concepts.intuition: A guesser that knows how common each topic is but never reads the article.
concepts.technical: Expected accuracy $= \sum_k p_k^2$, where $p_k$ is the fraction of class k. The book's empirical estimate on Reuters test labels is 0.1866.
concepts.significance: Provides the floor any useful model must beat.
concepts.misconception: The random baseline for K classes is not always 1/K; it equals 1/K only when classes are balanced.

concepts.name: Stopping at the best epoch
concepts.definition: Training only as many epochs as the validation curves indicate, before overfitting begins.
concepts.intuition: Stop studying the practice questions when your score on new questions stops improving.
concepts.technical: Done manually here: choose 9 epochs from figure 4.6, then retrain from scratch.
concepts.significance: One of the simplest ways to limit overfitting; chapter 5 covers more (p.138 mentions this).
concepts.misconception: Continuing the old 20-epoch model would not undo its overfitting; it must be rebuilt.

concepts.name: Overfitting
concepts.definition: Performance on training data keeps improving while performance on unseen data stops improving or worsens.
concepts.technical: Identified at about epoch 9 for this model from validation loss.
concepts.significance: Determines the retraining length on this page.
concepts.misconception: That overfitting only matters for huge models; this 647k-parameter model on 8k samples overfits within ten epochs.

math.title: Expected accuracy of a shuffled-label baseline
math.source_text: hits_array = np.array(test_labels == test_labels_copy); hits_array.mean() → 0.18655387355298308 (the closed form is not in the book)

variables.meaning: Fraction of test samples whose label is topic k
Number of test samples with label k

math.operations: Probability that a random label drawn at the class frequencies equals the true label: for each class, $p_k$ (true label is k) times $p_k$ (guess is k), summed over classes.
math.purpose: Explains why the empirical baseline on the page comes out near 19% rather than $1/46$.
math.interpretation: Imbalance raises the random baseline: a few large classes contribute most of $\sum p_k^2$.
math.intuition: If one topic made up 40% of the data, randomly guessing at base rates would already be right $0.4^2=16\%$ of the time from that topic alone.
math.numerical_example: Balanced 46 classes: $46\cdot(1/46)^2 = 1/46 \approx 0.022$. Two classes 50/50: 0.5. If classes had shares 0.35, 0.22 and 43 classes sharing the remaining 0.43 equally (≈0.01 each): $0.1225+0.0484+43\cdot0.0001\approx 0.175$, close to the book's 0.187.

math.title: Improvement over the baseline

variables.meaning: Test accuracy of the nine-epoch model

math.operations: Ratio and difference of the two accuracies printed on the page.
math.interpretation: The model is correct about 4.3 times as often as the random guesser, an absolute gain of 61 points.
math.intuition: Comparing against a baseline turns a raw number into evidence that the model learned something.

code.title: Retraining a model from scratch
code.original_code:
model = keras.Sequential(
    [
        layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
        layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
        layers.Dense(46, activation="softmax"),
    ]
)
model.compile(
    optimizer="adam",
    loss="categorical_crossentropy",
    metrics=["accuracy"],
)
model.fit(
    x_train,
    y_train,
    epochs=9,
    batch_size=512,
)
results = model.evaluate(x_test, y_test)
code.what_it_does: Builds a fresh 64-64-46 model, compiles it, trains it for nine epochs on all 8,982 training samples, and evaluates it on the 2,246 test samples.

line_explanations.explanation: Same architecture as listing 4.15; creating a new `Sequential` gives new random weights. (Printed as `ke ras.Sequential` because of a typesetting artifact.)
Adam + categorical crossentropy; only plain accuracy is tracked this time.
Train on the full training set for 9 epochs, batch size 512; no `validation_data`, since the hyperparameter is already chosen.

code.algorithm: Mini-batch training with Adam for 9 × 18 = 162 updates (8,982 / 512 → 17 full batches + 1 of 278), then a forward pass over the test set.
code.theory_link: Final evaluation on never-seen data after hyperparameter selection on the validation set.

code.title: Empirical random baseline
code.original_code:
>>> import copy
>>> test_labels_copy = copy.copy(test_labels)
>>> np.random.shuffle(test_labels_copy)
>>> hits_array = np.array(test_labels == test_labels_copy)
>>> hits_array.mean()
0.18655387355298308
code.what_it_does: Estimates the accuracy of a random classifier that respects class frequencies by comparing the true test labels with a randomly permuted copy.

line_explanations.explanation: Make a copy of the integer test labels so shuffling does not modify the originals.
Shuffle the copy in place; class counts are preserved, order is random.
Element-wise comparison gives a boolean array of length 2,246 (True where the shuffled label happens to match).
The mean of booleans is the fraction of matches: about 0.187.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: `test_labels`, integer array of length 2,246 (from p.141). Output: ≈0.1866.
code.algorithm: Monte Carlo estimate (one sample) of $\sum_k p_k^2$.
pitfalls: Without the copy, `np.random.shuffle(test_labels)` would scramble the real labels.
This uses the integer labels, not the one-hot `y_test`; shuffling a 2-D array would permute rows, and `==` would compare element-wise across 46 columns.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: closed-form version of the same baseline, not in the book
import numpy as np
counts = np.bincount(test_labels, minlength=46)
p = counts / counts.sum()
print((p ** 2).sum())          # close to 0.187
print(p.max())                 # accuracy of always predicting the most common topic

deeper.title: Two kinds of trivial baselines
deeper.body: Beyond the book: the shuffled-label baseline guesses at base rates. Another common trivial baseline is the **majority-class** classifier, which always predicts the most frequent topic and scores $\max_k p_k$. For imbalanced data the majority baseline is higher than the random one (since $\sum p_k^2 \le \max_k p_k$), so it is the tougher floor to beat. The book's 19% is the random version.

deeper.title: The full workflow on one page
deeper.body: 1. Hold out validation data and overtrain (p.144). 2. Read curves to pick the epoch count (p.145-146). 3. Rebuild the model and train on all training data for that many epochs (listing 4.22). 4. Evaluate once on the test set. 5. Compare with a baseline. The book uses the same sequence for IMDb (p.135-139).

takeaways: Overfitting starts after about nine epochs, so a fresh model is trained for nine epochs.
The final model is trained on all 8,982 training samples, without a validation split.
A shuffled-label random classifier gets ≈ 0.19, not 1/46, because the classes are imbalanced.
Always interpret a metric against a trivial baseline.

questions.question: Why do the authors build a new model in listing 4.22 instead of reusing the one trained in listing 4.18?
options: The old model has a different architecture
The old model was trained 20 epochs and is overfitted; a fresh model trained for 9 epochs avoids that
Keras models cannot be evaluated after fit() with validation_data
The new model uses sparse labels
questions.answer: The old model was trained 20 epochs and is overfitted; a fresh model trained for 9 epochs avoids that
questions.explanation: The architecture is identical, Keras can evaluate any trained model, and listing 4.22 still uses one-hot labels with categorical crossentropy.

questions.question: What do the two numbers in `[0.9565213431445807, 0.79697239536954589]` represent?
questions.answer: Test loss (categorical crossentropy ≈ 0.96) and test accuracy (≈ 0.797).
questions.explanation: `evaluate()` returns the loss followed by the compiled metrics; only `"accuracy"` was compiled.

questions.question: Three classes have shares 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2. What accuracy would the book's shuffled-label baseline give on average?
questions.explanation: A random match requires the shuffled label to equal the true one; for class k this happens with probability $p_k$ given the true label is k, so the expectation is $\sum_k p_k^2$ (AI explanation of the book's empirical method).

questions.question: Why is the random baseline for Reuters around 19% rather than about 2%?
questions.answer: Because the 46 topics are not equally represented; a few large topics dominate, so random guesses at base rates often hit them.
questions.explanation: The book states the classes "may not be equally represented" and measures 0.1866 empirically; the formula $\sum p_k^2$ explains the value.

questions.question: Why does the baseline code use `copy.copy(test_labels)` before shuffling?
options: Because np.random.shuffle works only on copies
Because np.random.shuffle shuffles in place, and the original labels must stay intact for the comparison
questions.answer: Because np.random.shuffle shuffles in place, and the original labels must stay intact for the comparison
questions.explanation: Shuffling the original would leave nothing to compare against. Copying does not one-hot encode, shuffle works on any array, and reproducibility would need a seed.

questions.question: Listing 4.22 trains on `x_train` rather than `partial_x_train`. What changes, and is the nine-epoch choice still exactly right?
questions.answer: It uses all 8,982 samples (1,000 more), giving 18 updates per epoch instead of 16. The nine-epoch choice is a good approximation but not exact, since more data and more updates per epoch can shift the best stopping point slightly.
questions.explanation: Using all data for the final model is standard once hyperparameters are fixed; the remark about the shift is an AI explanation, not in the book.

questions.question: Can you explain in two sentences to a colleague why 80% accuracy on Reuters is good, using the numbers on this page?
questions.answer: A classifier that guesses topics at their natural frequencies gets about 19%; the model gets about 80%, more than four times as often correct, so it is clearly extracting topic information from the text.
questions.explanation: This is the comparison the authors make at the bottom of the page.
